summary:
Guinea is a high-risk destination for transgender visitors. Article 274 of the 2016 Penal Code punishes consensual same-sex conduct with six months to three years' imprisonment, a fine of GNF 500,000 to 1,000,000, or both; the predecessor provision, Article 325 of the 1998 Penal Code, criminalised the same conduct and carried a lower minimum fine. Where violence or attempted violence is involved, sentences rise to five to ten years, and acts with a person under 21 trigger the maximum penalty.

Enforcement does not depend on conduct alone. Police arrest people on the basis of clothing and appearance, and Article 274 operates as a standing basis for extortion, with release commonly secured by payment to officers. A 2024 Universal Periodic Review stakeholder submission reports LGBTQ people held for up to five days despite the 48-hour legal limit, most released only after paying bribes or fines.

Transgender women face a specific and documented pattern: arrest and imprisonment on the stated pretext of protecting them from community violence, followed by detention in male prisons where they frequently experience sexual violence. The US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report records violence and discrimination against LGBT persons and police harassment under the code's indecency provisions, and the Advocates for Human Rights and Khaleem Ali joint stakeholder report of October 2024 describes a hostile and sometimes lethal environment in which stigma and fear deter reporting of violence. In 2023 the Office for the Protection of Women, Children, and Morals added a unit to investigate same-sex conduct.

There is no legal gender recognition in Guinea and no recognition of same-sex unions. No sourced material establishes entry screening procedures, visa rules or border checks specific to trans or LGBTQ travellers; the only relevant instrument is Section 9.9.30(b) of the 2022 Guinea Aeronautical Regulations, issued by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, which bars competent government agencies from using Passenger Name Record data revealing an individual's sex life or sexual orientation. The text gives no further detail on how that bar operates in practice.
tangentialFactors:
Official hostility has been stated at the highest level. In 2010 Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate declared that consensual same-sex activity was wrong and should be illegal, and that sexual orientation should not be a human right. The 2023 US State Department report found that LGBT people are cast as part of a Western imperialist agenda attributed to the United States and France, a framing that shapes how a foreign visitor's gender presentation may be read.

The trajectory recorded by external monitors is one of continued criminalisation with hardened enforcement machinery. The 2011 US State Department report described homosexuality as socially, religiously and culturally taboo, with no LGBTQ organisations in the country; by 2023 LGBTQ groups existed but could not obtain legal recognition despite no law barring it, most LGBTQ Guineans did not disclose publicly, and there was no substantial political presence of openly LGBTQ people.

Two statutes place transgender people on paper within a defined category. Law L/2024/001/CNT/SGG of 12 January 2024 on HIV Prevention, Care, and Protection defines members of sexual minorities to include gays, lesbians, bisexuals, intersex and transgender people whether or not they self-identify, and Ordinance No. 056/2009/PRG/SGG on HIV/AIDS lists sexual minorities as a vulnerable and marginalised group. Neither statute provides protection against discrimination, and no law bars LGBTQ people from discrimination in health services.

A survey spanning 2021 to 2023 found that 87 percent of Guineans would dislike or strongly dislike having a gay neighbour, an indicator of the ambient risk a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor carries. Some LGBTQ Guineans have been internally displaced to escape areas whose religious and cultural norms endanger them.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ people in Guinea face discrimination when seeking healthcare, housing, education and employment, and the HIV statutes naming sexual minorities as a vulnerable group carry no enforceable non-discrimination duty. Families arrange forced heterosexual marriages, and religious, cultural and familial pressure is used in attempts to convert LGBTQ people, pressure that falls heaviest on younger people.

Abuse in custody is reported as routine: LGBTQ people held in detention are frequently abused, and the arrest and male-prison placement of transgender women described in stakeholder submissions is presented as a recurring practice rather than an isolated case. Deepening stigma and fear among LGBT people are recorded in the October 2024 UPR stakeholder reporting as a direct consequence of police arbitrary arrest, harassment and extortion.

Family law permits adoption by a couple married at least five years or by an unmarried person aged at least 30, subject to a 15-year age gap, and Guinean law does not specifically bar LGBTQ persons from adopting. In 2016 and 2017 the organisation Afrique Arc-en-Ciel Conakry reported gay men jailed and then fined to secure their release. The US State Department's 2011 report noted that LGBTQ organisations did not exist; the 2023 report noted that groups do exist but cannot obtain legal recognition, and that most LGBTQ Guineans do not disclose their identity publicly.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not establish entry screening procedures, visa rules, passport or marker requirements, or border-check practice for trans or LGBTQ travellers to Guinea. The 2022 aeronautical regulation barring government use of Passenger Name Record data on sex life or sexual orientation gives no operational detail, and its effect on actual screening is unresolved.

Two provisions are cited across sources for the same offence: Article 274 of the 2016 Penal Code and Article 325 of the 1998 Penal Code. Which text currently governs prosecutions, and whether both remain operative, is not resolved by the inventory.

Whether the unit added within the Office for the Protection of Women, Children, and Morals in 2023 has produced prosecutions, and the scale of its activity, is not sourced. Prison conditions for detained transgender women rest on stakeholder and secondary reporting rather than official or independently verified inspection material. Claims about internal displacement of LGBTQ Guineans and about conversion pressure come from stakeholder submissions without corroborating quantitative data.
